original_question: Is there a more elaborate duality theory relating real Hopf algebras and weakly complete Hopf algebras in which the pro-Lie group and pro-Lie algebra facts described in the paper play an essential role, and does the existence of weakly complete enveloping algebras of weakly complete Lie algebras imply that for every pro-Lie algebra L there is an associative weakly complete Hopf algebra U(L) such that L is isomorphic to a closed Lie subalgebra of the primitive elements P(U(L))?
correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper’s actual target. It correctly identifies the open problem asked immediately after the Hopf-algebra discussion in Section 8, and it preserves both parts of Question 6: (i) a duality theory between real Hopf algebras and weakly-complete Hopf algebras in which the pro-Lie group/pro-Lie algebra facts just proved are genuinely used, and (ii) the existence, for each pro-Lie algebra L, of an associative weakly-complete Hopf algebra U(L) such that L is isomorphic to a closed Lie subalgebra of the primitive elements P(U(L)).
missing_details: The paper is working over the real numbers: 'real Hopf algebras' are group objects in the category V of real vector spaces, and pro-Lie algebras are real topological Lie algebras.

To make the question stand-alone, 'weakly-complete' should be specified: a weakly-complete topological vector space is one isomorphic to R^I with the product topology, equivalently to Hom(E,R) for some real vector space E.
A 'weakly-complete Hopf algebra' should be identified as a group object in the category W of weakly-complete real topological vector spaces with completed tensor product ⊗e.

The phrase 'the pro-Lie group and pro-Lie algebra facts described in the paper' should be unpacked as the content of Theorem 19: for a weakly-complete Hopf algebra A, G(A) is a pro-Lie group, P(A) is a pro-Lie algebra, and the restricted exponential map exp_A|P(A): P(A) → G(A) is the exponential map of G(A).
The notation P(U(L)) should be defined explicitly as the primitive elements: P(U(L)) = {x in U(L) : c(x) = x ⊗e 1 + 1 ⊗e x}.
The intended isomorphism is not merely algebraic: L should be isomorphic as a topological Lie algebra to a closed Lie subalgebra of P(U(L)).
The official formulation in the paper is a two-part open question, Question 6(i)-(ii); your draft compresses the two subquestions into one sentence.
refined_question: Working over R, let V be the category of real vector spaces with the usual tensor product and W the dual category of weakly-complete real topological vector spaces with completed tensor product ⊗e. If A is a weakly-complete Hopf algebra (that is, a group object in W), write G(A) for its grouplike elements and P(A) = {x in A : c(x) = x ⊗e 1 + 1 ⊗e x} for its primitive elements. Since Theorem 19 shows that G(A) is a pro-Lie group, P(A) is its pro-Lie algebra, and exp_A restricted to P(A) is the exponential map, is there a more elaborate duality theory between real Hopf algebras and weakly-complete Hopf algebras in which these pro-Lie group and pro-Lie algebra features play a role; and, in particular, does the existence of weakly-complete enveloping algebras for weakly-complete Lie algebras imply that every real pro-Lie algebra L admits an associative weakly-complete Hopf algebra U(L) such that L is isomorphic, as a topological Lie algebra, to a closed Lie subalgebra of P(U(L))?
justification: The draft is targeting the exact open problem asked in Section 8, Question 6, not an earlier structural theorem. The introduction explicitly says that Section 8 treats the appearance of pro-Lie groups in character theory of Hopf algebras. Section 8 then sets up the real-versus-weakly-complete categorical framework, defines weakly-complete Hopf algebras and the sets G(A) and P(A), proves the key pro-Lie statement for them in Theorem 19, interprets G(A) as a character group when A is dual to an abstract Hopf algebra, and immediately asks Question 6. So the closest paper-faithful target is exactly Question 6(i)-(ii), with the notation and scope supplied by Definition 5, Definition 6, Theorem 18, and Theorem 19.
